claims.text: Adding less than 1 wt% Hf to a NiCoCrFeAl-based bond coat and homogenizing it at approximately 1150°C will improve bond-coat durability and reliability.
The proposed homogenization treatment will produce a uniform Hf distribution.
Hf will segregate to grain boundaries in the treated NiCoCrFeAl-based alloy.
The treatment will form stable, fine Hf-oxide precipitates at grain boundaries.
The Hf-oxide precipitates will act as grain-boundary pinning sites.
Hf-oxide precipitates will impede grain-boundary diffusion.
Hf-oxide precipitates will impede crack initiation.
Hf will enhance oxidation resistance by forming a protective oxide on grain boundaries.
The proposed mechanism will stabilize the bond-coat microstructure during high-temperature oxidation.
The Hf-doped bond coat will exhibit less oxidation-induced degradation than the untreated alloy.
The Hf-doped bond coat will have greater grain-boundary stability than the untreated alloy.
The Hf-doped bond coat will have greater durability and reliability during cyclic high-temperature exposure than the untreated alloy.
Untreated NiCoCrFeAl-based bond coats undergo typical oxidation and grain-boundary weakening at high temperatures.
The treatment should remain effective during prolonged cyclic oxidation near 1150°C under controlled oxygen partial pressure.
Nonuniform Hf distribution may limit the treatment's effectiveness.
Excessive Hf may produce brittle phases and limit the treatment's effectiveness.
The optimal treatment may depend on alloy composition and service geometry.
Reactive-element microalloying is a well-supported mechanism for this application.
Optimal homogenization conditions are uncertain because local Hf concentration peaks and long-term instability may occur.
Failure of the Hf-treated specimens to show statistically significant improvements over untreated controls would falsify the hypothesis.
